standard.title: Develop, evaluate and recommend strategies
standard.description: develop and evaluate strategies using environmental, economic or social criteria; recommend a strategy and explain the predicted impacts
standard.prior_knowledge: At Y9, students developed and evaluated strategies using environmental, economic or social criteria, recommended a strategy and explained predicted impacts (AC9HG9S05). At Y10 the same descriptor applies with greater complexity: explicit reflection on personal values, evaluation of collective as well as individual action, and integration with First Nations traditional practices.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop and evaluate both individual and collective strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; recommend a strategy with explained predicted impacts; reflect on personal values and their influence on strategy choices.

nodes.label: Developing strategies — individual and collective
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can propose both individual and collective strategies for addressing a geographical challenge, supporting each with reasons.
nodes.minimum_width: Propose at least one individual and one collective strategy for a geographical challenge, providing reasons for each.
nodes.typical_width: Propose and describe both individual actions (e.g. reducing ecological footprint) and collective actions (e.g. community programs, volunteering, policy advocacy) for a geographical challenge; explain the reasoning behind each strategy and identify who is responsible for implementation.
wider: Investigate specific organisations that students could engage with collectively — Red Cross, Red Crescent, environmental NGOs — and evaluate what individual participation in collective action achieves
Compare the scale and type of impact achievable through individual vs collective action for the same challenge, identifying where individual action is most and least effective
Research a case where grassroots collective action led to policy change, tracing the pathway from individual decisions to collective impact at a systems level

response_modes.reason: Students often focus on individual action as the primary response to geographical challenges. Exposure to collective action models — including First Nations community-led approaches — broadens the strategy repertoire.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The individual/collective distinction maps onto different modes of geographical agency — students who have explored both develop a more nuanced understanding of how change happens at different scales.
success_criteria: Students propose at least one individual and one collective strategy, providing reasons for each
Students identify who has responsibility for implementing each proposed strategy

nodes.label: Evaluating strategies against criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy using environmental, economic and social criteria, reflecting on whether the strategy achieves its aims.
nodes.minimum_width: Evaluate one strategy against at least two criteria (environmental, economic or social), identifying evidence of effectiveness and limitations.
nodes.typical_width: Evaluate strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; reflect on whether environmental degradation has been reduced or wellbeing improved; explain reasons for decisions including traditional practices (e.g. firestick farming) and grassroots aid implementations.
wider: Apply a systematic multi-criteria evaluation framework to compare two strategies for the same challenge, producing a reasoned recommendation based on the comparison
Examine cases where evaluation evidence for a strategy is contested — identifying why different evaluators reach different conclusions using the same criteria

Evaluate a strategy involving First Nations traditional practices (e.g. firestick farming, water management) against environmental, cultural and social criteria — explaining how traditional practices are validated as effective strategies
nodes.hinge_reason: Multi-criteria evaluation is the basis for the recommendation in Node 3 — if students evaluate using only one criterion or apply criteria without evidence, their recommendation will not be genuinely justified and the final integration node cannot produce a defensible geographical conclusion.

response_modes.reason: Students often evaluate using one preferred criterion (usually environmental or economic) and ignore the others. Scaffold simultaneous three-criteria evaluation explicitly — including acknowledgment that criteria may point in different directions and that trade-offs are a feature, not a problem to be resolved.

success_criteria: Students evaluate a strategy against at least two criteria from different domains, providing evidence for their evaluation
Students identify at least one trade-off in the strategy — where meeting one criterion compromises another

nodes.label: Recommending a strategy with predicted impacts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recommend a strategy, explain the predicted impacts, and reflect on how personal values and attitudes influence the strategy choice.
nodes.minimum_width: Recommend one strategy, explain at least two predicted impacts, and reflect on how at least one personal value influenced the choice.
nodes.typical_width: Recommend a strategy supported by reasons from the evaluation; explain predicted environmental, economic and social impacts; reflect on how personal values and attitudes — including sustainability values, social justice values or cultural values — influenced the strategy choice.
wider: Develop a recommendation that explicitly addresses the trade-offs identified in Node 2 — explaining how the recommended strategy prioritises some criteria over others and why
Reflect on how a different value position would lead to a different strategy recommendation — making the value-strategy connection explicit and non-deterministic
Apply sustainable design principles to an urban or built environment strategy and explain how the design principles reflect specific values about wellbeing, environment and community

response_modes.reason: A strategy recommendation integrates criteria evaluation, predicted impact analysis and value reflection into a coherent geographical argument. The teaching signal is to make each component explicit in the recommendation — not a bare recommendation, but one that shows the evaluative reasoning and value position behind it.

success_criteria: Students recommend a strategy and explain at least two predicted impacts (one intended, one possible unintended or trade-off consequence)
Students reflect on at least one personal value that influenced their strategy choice, explaining the connection
